## Start here

`Kosha()` opens two indexes, the repo index (`.kosha/code.db`) and the
index of installed packages (`kosha/env.db` in the user data directory),
plus the call graph over both. Check that they are current before
trusting an answer, because code missing from a stale index looks the
same as code that does not exist:

``` python
from kosha import Kosha
k = Kosha()
k.status()
# {'files': 4, 'packages': 355, 'graph_nodes': 10630, 'stale_files': 0, 'stale_pkgs': {'httpx': '0.28.1'}, 'new_files': 0}
```

Sync only when something you need is stale. Computing embeddings for
changed code is the one slow step:

``` python
k.sync()                            # repo, stale packages and call graph
k.sync(embed=False)                 # store new chunks without embeddings: keyword search only, much faster
k.sync(pkgs=['httpx'], repo=False)  # one package
```

Then search. `context` is the default and searches both indexes;
`env_context` and `repo_context` search one each and are faster:

``` python
for r in k.env_context('atomic file write preserving permissions', limit=8):
    print(r['metadata']['mod_name'], r['metadata'].get('lineno'), r['content'][:120])
```

`pkg_context` searches package descriptions, one per indexed package, to
find a package by what it does. `doc(Kosha)` lists every method with its
signature; the table is a map, not the full reference. Indexing
(`update_repo`, `update_pkgs`, `process_env`) and deleting (`nuke`,
`rm_pkg`, `prune_old_pkgs`) are methods of the same class, but `sync` is
the only one you normally need.

## Filters

Filters go inside the query string, next to the plain words, and work
with `context`, `env_context` and `repo_context`.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
<col style="width: 25%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Token</th>
<th>Aliases</th>
<th>Example</th>
<th>Effect</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>package:</code></td>
<td><code>pkg:</code>, <code>packages:</code>, <code>pkgs:</code></td>
<td><code>package:fastcore</code></td>
<td>one package</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>path:</code></td>
<td><code>dir:</code>, <code>folder:</code>, <code>paths:</code></td>
<td><code>path:xtras</code></td>
<td>path contains the text</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>file:</code></td>
<td><code>filename:</code>, <code>files:</code></td>
<td><code>file:xtras*</code></td>
<td>path matches the glob</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>lang:</code></td>
<td><code>ext:</code>, <code>extension:</code>, <code>langs:</code></td>
<td><code>lang:py</code></td>
<td>language, by file extension</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>type:</code></td>
<td><code>types:</code></td>
<td><code>type:FunctionDef</code></td>
<td>kind of definition</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Separate several values with commas to accept any of them
(`package:httpx,requests`). Every filter excludes code that does not
match, and a trailing `!` (`package!:x`) means the same as without it.
In `context`, a `package:` filter also skips the repo search. A package
name written as a plain word, as in `k.context('fastcore atomic save')`,
is not a filter: it ranks that package’s hits higher, and other packages
still appear.

A filter-shaped token with an unknown key is reported in
`parseq(q)[1]['_unknown']`, and the command line prints a warning. The
token is searched as plain text, so a typo such as `libr:litesearch`
would otherwise return a full page of results that ignore the filter you
meant.

## Reading a result

``` python
{'content':  'def merge(*ds):\n    "Merge all dicts"\n    ...',
 'metadata': {'mod_name': 'fastcore.basics.merge',   # the name to pass to ni() and short_path()
              'path': '.../fastcore/basics.py', 'lineno': 655,
              'type': 'FunctionDef', 'package': 'fastcore',
              'public_api': True, 'docstring': 'Merge all dicts'},
 'pagerank': 0.00027, 'in_degree': 8, 'out_degree': 12,
 'callers': [...], 'callees': [...], 'co_dispatched': []}
```

`pagerank` measures how much code depends on a node. Changing a node
with a high score affects more code, so look at its callers first.
`callers` shows where the code is used, and `callees` shows what it uses
that you might reuse.

`co_dispatched` is the least obvious field and often the most useful. It
lists the functions assigned together with this one in a module-level
list, dict or tuple: route tables, handler maps, plugin registries. When
you add another handler, it names the existing ones and so shows where
they are registered, without reading the glue code.

The graph fields appear only when `graph=True`, the default for
`context`. `env_context` and `repo_context` return `content` and
`metadata` only.

## The call graph

`k.graph` is the graph itself, a `CodeGraph` built from ast-grep static
analysis plus Python AST rules for decorators, registrations and
`@patch`. Besides the methods above it has
`k.graph.ranked(k=10, module='fastcore')`, `k.graph.callers`,
`k.graph.file2nodes` and `k.graph.co_dispatched`; `doc(k.graph)` lists
them all.

Node names are the dotted `mod_name` from a hit’s metadata. A name that
is not in the graph gives an empty result, not an error, so an empty
`short_path` means either that there is no path or that a node is not
indexed. Check `k.ni(name)` before concluding that two pieces of code do
not connect.

## Long-form docs

Code chunks suit code, not prose. `k.docs` is a separate index for
READMEs and documentation folders, a litesearch `Index` that splits
documents by heading. It is created the first time you use it:

``` python
k.add_pkg_docs('fastcore')          # a package's full README
k.add_docs('path/to/docs')          # a folder, a file, or {title: text}
k.docs_context('how do I install')  # ranked sections, each with a node_id
k.docs.read(node_id)['text']        # one whole section
```

`docs_context(q, sections=False)` returns raw chunks instead. The docs
index does not track staleness: adding a changed document again stores
the new text but does not remove the old version.

## Reranking

`context`, `env_context`, `repo_context` and `pkg_context` take
`rerank=True`, which reorders the hits with a flashrank cross-encoder, a
small model that scores each hit against the query. The first call
downloads the model. Reranking reorders what was retrieved and never
adds to it.

It is off by default. It helps most when the query uses the same words
as the target’s docstring. When a query is phrased differently, the
right code is usually missing from the candidates in the first place,
and reordering cannot bring it back. `context` reranks only its final
top hits; `env_context` and `repo_context` first retrieve a wider pool
for the reranker to choose from.

## Outside Python

The same index can be reached in three other ways, for callers that are
not Python processes:

- Command line: `kosha sync`,
  `kosha context 'query' --limit 10 --rerank`, `kosha ni <mod_name>`,
  `kosha public-api <pkg>`, and `--as-json` on any of them for JSON
  output.
- Daemon: `kosha daemon` keeps one embedding model loaded and reads
  `{"cmd": ..., "args": {...}}` requests as JSON lines on standard
  input, which saves the few seconds of loading on every call.
- MCP: `kosha-mcp` offers the same operations as MCP tools over stdio.
  If the host already has it configured, call those tools instead of
  importing anything.

## The indexes are litesearch databases

`k.codedb` and `k.envdb` are litesearch databases, so the whole
litesearch API works on them: extra tables, raw SQL, custom stores.

``` python
list(k.envdb.q("select content from store where json_extract(metadata,'$.mod_name') = ?", ['fastcore.basics.merge']))
summaries = k.envdb.get_store(name='summaries')   # for example, notes an agent writes about undocumented code
```

Embeddings are stored and read back as 16-bit floats.
[`kosha.core.cast_emb`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kosha/core.html#cast_emb)
enforces that, so a custom embedding function cannot write a wider type
by mistake.

``` python
from pyskills import doc, xdir, list_pyskills
import kosha.skill

# the entry point resolves, and its blurb is the first paragraph of the module docstring
assert 'kosha.skill' in list_pyskills(), list_pyskills().keys()
assert set(xdir(kosha.skill)) >= {'Kosha', 'CodeGraph', 'pkg_url'}  # plus the sibling submodules pyskills adds
print(list_pyskills()['kosha.skill'])
```

    Search your repo and every installed package by meaning, then follow the call graph between them. Use it before you grep, open a source file, or write code a dependency already provides. Keyword search, vector search and a static call graph over local SQLite, with no LLM calls and no network.

``` python
# every method the docstring points at exists, so a harness following it can't hit an AttributeError
named = ['status','sync','context','env_context','repo_context','pkg_context','docs_context','public_api',
         'top_nodes','api_call_paths','dep_stack','where_to_add','ni','neighbors','short_path','add_docs','add_pkg_docs']
missing = [m for m in named if not hasattr(Kosha, m)]
assert not missing, f'skill docstring names methods Kosha does not have: {missing}'
gmissing = [m for m in ['ranked','callers','callees','co_dispatched','file2nodes','node_info'] if not hasattr(CodeGraph, m)]
assert not gmissing, gmissing
doc(kosha.skill)
```
